q: A Bill is deemed to be a Money Bill, within the meaning of the Constitution, if it contains only provisions dealing with the matters specified in:

options.A: Article 110 of the Constitution
options.B: Article 112 of the Constitution
options.C: Article 114 of the Constitution
options.D: Article 266 of the Constitution

e: Article 110 contains the exhaustive list of Money Bill matters, such as taxation, Government borrowing and matters relating to the Consolidated Fund; a Bill containing only such provisions is deemed to be a Money Bill.

q:
Consider the following statements:
1. The salaries and allowances payable to the Judges of a High Court are charged on the Consolidated Fund of the State concerned.
2. The pensions payable to or in respect of the Judges of a High Court are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 1 only
options.B: 2 only
options.C: Both 1 and 2
options.D: Neither 1 nor 2

e: Both statements are correct: the salary of a High Court Judge is charged on the Consolidated Fund of the State, whereas the pension payable to or in respect of such a Judge is charged on the Consolidated Fund of India.

q: Grants-in-aid to the States under Article 275 of the Constitution are:

options.A: Charged on the Consolidated Fund of India
options.B: Voted by the Lok Sabha as part of the Demands for Grants
options.C: Paid out of the Public Account of India
options.D: Paid out of the Contingency Fund of India

e: Grants-in-aid under Article 275 are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India, so the sums provided by Parliament by law for States in need of assistance are not voted like ordinary Demands.

q: Besides the items of expenditure specified in Article 112(3) of the Constitution, other expenditure can be treated as 'charged' on the Consolidated Fund of India where:

options.A: The Finance Minister so directs
options.B: The Public Accounts Committee so recommends
options.C: The Comptroller and Auditor General so certifies
options.D: It is declared by the Constitution or by Parliament by law to be so charged

e: The closing words of Article 112(3) allow other expenditure to be charged only where the Constitution itself or Parliament by law so declares; no executive authority can create a new charged item.

q: Under Article 266(2) of the Constitution, all public moneys received by or on behalf of the Government of India, other than the revenues and loans credited to the Consolidated Fund, shall be credited to:

options.A: The Public Account of India
options.B: The Contingency Fund of India
options.C: The Consolidated Fund of the State concerned
options.D: A deposit account with the Reserve Bank of India

e: Article 266(2) directs that all public moneys other than the revenues and loans credited to the Consolidated Fund, such as deposits and remittances, shall be credited to the Public Account of India.

q: Under Article 279 of the Constitution, the 'net proceeds' of a tax or duty, for the purpose of distribution between the Union and the States, are ascertained and certified by:

options.A: The Finance Commission
options.B: The Ministry of Finance
options.C: The Comptroller and Auditor General of India, whose certificate is final
options.D: The Reserve Bank of India

e: Under Article 279, the net proceeds of a tax or duty meant for distribution between the Union and the States are ascertained and certified by the Comptroller and Auditor General, whose certificate is final.

q:
Consider the following statements:
1. The proceeds of a surcharge on taxes levied by the Union under Article 271 of the Constitution form part of the Consolidated Fund of India and are not shared with the States.
2. A cess levied for specific purposes is likewise excluded from the divisible pool of taxes shared with the States.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 1 only
options.B: 2 only
options.C: Both 1 and 2
options.D: Neither 1 nor 2

e: Both are correct: a surcharge under Article 271 is levied for Union purposes and forms no part of the sharable pool, and a cess levied for specific purposes is likewise excluded from the divisible pool.

q: The recommendations of the Finance Commission constituted under Article 280 of the Constitution are:

options.A: Binding on the Government of India
options.B: Enforceable by the Supreme Court
options.C: Advisory in character, and not binding on the Government
options.D: Binding only in respect of the States

e: The Finance Commission's recommendations are advisory in character; the Government acts on them largely by convention, but they are not legally binding and cannot be enforced by a court.

q: The oath or affirmation made by the Comptroller and Auditor General of India before entering upon his office is in the form set out for the purpose in:

options.A: The Third Schedule to the Constitution
options.B: The First Schedule to the Constitution
options.C: The Comptroller and Auditor General's (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971
options.D: The General Financial Rules

e: The form of oath or affirmation to be made by the Comptroller and Auditor General before entering upon his office is set out in the Third Schedule to the Constitution.

q: A Vote on Account, by which grants are made in advance in respect of the estimated expenditure for a part of the financial year, is generally passed by the Lok Sabha:

options.A: After detailed examination of the estimates by the Estimates Committee
options.B: Only after the Appropriation Bill is passed
options.C: After the Demands are examined by the Public Accounts Committee
options.D: Without detailed discussion of the estimates, pending their detailed consideration

e: A Vote on Account is passed by the Lok Sabha without detailed discussion of the estimates, so that funds are available for the opening months pending detailed consideration and voting of the Demands.

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes a Vote on Account from an advance out of the Contingency Fund of India?

options.A: A Vote on Account is an advance made by the executive, while the Contingency Fund advance is voted by Parliament
options.B: A Vote on Account is a grant voted by the Lok Sabha in advance for a part of the year, while an advance from the Contingency Fund is made by the executive to meet unforeseen expenditure pending authorisation by Parliament
options.C: Both are made by the executive without the vote of Parliament
options.D: There is no difference between the two

e: A Vote on Account is a grant actually voted by the Lok Sabha in advance for part of the year, whereas a Contingency Fund advance is made by the executive for unforeseen expenditure and is recouped after Parliament authorises the expenditure.

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes an 'exceptional grant' from a 'vote of credit'?

options.A: An exceptional grant is made for a special purpose forming no part of the current service of any financial year, while a vote of credit is granted for an unexpected demand which, by reason of its magnitude or indefinite character, cannot be stated with the details ordinarily given in the Annual Financial Statement
options.B: An exceptional grant is voted after the year is over, while a vote of credit is voted in advance
options.C: An exceptional grant relates to charged expenditure, while a vote of credit relates to voted expenditure
options.D: There is no difference between the two

e: An exceptional grant finances a special purpose forming no part of the current service of any financial year, while a vote of credit meets an unexpected demand which, by reason of its magnitude or indefinite character, cannot be detailed in the usual form.

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes a Supplementary Grant from an Excess Grant?

options.A: A Supplementary Grant is voted after the close of the year, while an Excess Grant is voted during the year
options.B: A Supplementary Grant relates to charged expenditure only, while an Excess Grant relates to voted grants only
options.C: There is no difference between the two
options.D: A Supplementary Grant is voted during the financial year when the amount authorised for a service is found to be insufficient, while an Excess Grant is voted after the close of the year to regularise expenditure already incurred in excess of the grant

e: A Supplementary Grant is voted during the financial year when the amount authorised for a service proves insufficient, whereas an Excess Grant is voted after the year closes to regularise expenditure already incurred in excess of the grant.

q: Re-appropriation of funds from one grant (Demand) to another grant is:

options.A: Permissible with the sanction of the General Manager
options.B: Permissible with the concurrence of the FA&CAO
options.C: Permissible with the approval of the Railway Board
options.D: Not permissible, as re-appropriation can be made only within the same grant

e: Each grant is a separate vote of Parliament, so funds cannot be transferred from one grant to another; re-appropriation is permissible only between heads within the same grant.

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes 'surrender' of funds from 're-appropriation' of funds?

options.A: Surrender is a transfer of funds from one head to another within a grant, while re-appropriation is the return of savings to the Government
options.B: Surrender is the return of anticipated savings in a grant to the Government, while re-appropriation is the transfer of funds from one head of account to another within the same grant
options.C: Both mean the return of savings at the end of the year
options.D: There is no difference between the two

e: Surrender means giving up savings so that they cease to be available to the surrendering unit, whereas re-appropriation diverts savings under one head of a grant to meet expenditure under another head of the same grant.

q: The members of the Estimates Committee of Parliament hold office for a term of:

options.A: Five years
options.B: Three years
options.C: Two years
options.D: One year

e: The Estimates Committee is constituted afresh every year. Its members hold office for a term of one year, though they may be re-elected.

q: One of the functions of the Estimates Committee of Parliament is to:

options.A: Examine the accounts of public undertakings
options.B: Suggest alternative policies in order to bring about efficiency and economy in administration
options.C: Review the rate of dividend payable by Railways to General Finances
options.D: Certify the Appropriation Accounts of Railways

e: Besides examining whether money is well laid out, the Estimates Committee may suggest alternative policies in order to bring about efficiency and economy in administration.

q: The members of the Departmentally Related Standing Committees of Parliament are:

options.A: Elected by the two Houses by proportional representation
options.B: Nominated by the Speaker of the Lok Sabha and the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha from amongst the members of their respective Houses
options.C: Appointed by the President of India
options.D: Nominated by the Minister of Parliamentary Affairs

e: Members of the Departmentally Related Standing Committees are nominated by the Speaker of the Lok Sabha and the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha from amongst the members of their respective Houses.

q: The Departmentally Related Standing Committee on Railways does NOT ordinarily consider:

options.A: The Demands for Grants of the Ministry of Railways
options.B: The annual reports of the Ministry of Railways
options.C: National basic long-term policy documents presented to the Houses
options.D: Matters of day-to-day administration of the Ministry of Railways

e: These committees consider Demands for Grants, annual reports and long-term policy documents, but matters of day-to-day administration are expressly kept outside their consideration.

q: Under the framework of the International Standards of Supreme Audit Institutions (ISSAI), public-sector auditing comprises three broad types, namely:

options.A: Financial audit, performance audit and compliance audit
options.B: Internal audit, external audit and vigilance audit
options.C: Pre-audit, post-audit and concurrent audit
options.D: Central audit, local audit and resident audit

e: The ISSAI framework classifies public-sector auditing into three broad types: financial audit, performance audit and compliance audit.

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes statutory audit from internal audit in respect of reporting?

options.A: Statutory audit reports to the management of the Railway, while internal audit reports to Parliament
options.B: Both report to the Public Accounts Committee
options.C: Statutory audit by the Comptroller and Auditor General reports, through the President, to Parliament, while internal audit reports to the management of the Railway itself
options.D: There is no difference in their reporting

e: Statutory audit by the Comptroller and Auditor General reports, through the President, to Parliament, while internal audit is an instrument of the Railway's own management and reports to that management.

q:
Consider the following statements:
1. The internal check exercised by the Railway Accounts Department over claims and bills is a cent-per-cent check exercised before payment.
2. The audit exercised by the organisation of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India is a test check of selected transactions.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 1 only
options.B: 2 only
options.C: Both 1 and 2
options.D: Neither 1 nor 2

e: Both are correct: the internal check exercised by the Railway Accounts Department over claims and bills is a cent-per-cent check before payment, while the Comptroller and Auditor General's audit is a test check of selected transactions.

q: Performance audit conducted by the Comptroller and Auditor General of India is also popularly described as:

options.A: Propriety audit
options.B: Value-for-Money audit
options.C: Certification audit
options.D: Appropriation audit

e: Performance audit is popularly called Value-for-Money audit because it examines whether public expenditure has secured economy, efficiency and effectiveness, and not merely whether it was regular.

q: Which of the following correctly states the position of statutory audit in relation to Government policy?

options.A: Audit can set aside a policy of the Government which it considers wasteful
options.B: Audit frames the policy underlying each item of expenditure
options.C: Audit approval is required before a policy is implemented
options.D: Audit does not sit in judgment over Government policy itself, but examines the implementation of policy and the economy, efficiency and effectiveness of the expenditure incurred under it

e: Audit does not sit in judgment over Government policy itself; it examines the implementation of policy and the economy, efficiency and effectiveness of the expenditure incurred under it.

q: In audit parlance, an auditor is aptly described as:

options.A: A bloodhound, and not a watchdog
options.B: A watchdog, and not a bloodhound
options.C: An investigator of frauds only
options.D: A guarantor of the correctness of the accounts

e: The auditor is described as a watchdog and not a bloodhound: he guards the public purse on behalf of Parliament but proceeds without a presumption of dishonesty, unlike an investigator hunting for fraud.

q: A 'Provisional Para' in the audit objection process on Railways signifies:

options.A: The first objection raised in an Inspection Report
options.B: A paragraph already included in the Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General and examined by the Public Accounts Committee
options.C: A paragraph in the form in which it is proposed to be included in the Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General, communicated to the Ministry/Department for its final comments before the Report is finalised
options.D: A paragraph in the report of the internal audit organisation of the Railway

e: A Provisional Para is the paragraph in the form in which it is proposed to be included in the Comptroller and Auditor General's Report, communicated to the Ministry for its final comments before the Report is finalised.

q: In the case of a Government company, the statutory auditors are appointed by the Comptroller and Auditor General of India under the provisions of:

options.A: Section 139(5) of the Companies Act, 2013
options.B: Section 13 of the Comptroller and Auditor General's (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971
options.C: The General Financial Rules, 2017
options.D: The Railways Act, 1989

e: In the case of a Government company, the statutory auditors are appointed by the Comptroller and Auditor General under Section 139(5) of the Companies Act, 2013.

q: In the Balance Sheet of a Railway, a debit balance under a suspense head of account is shown:

options.A: On the liabilities side
options.B: As a deduction from the capital-at-charge
options.C: In the Public Account of India only
options.D: On the assets side, as it represents an amount recoverable by, or awaiting adjustment in favour of, the Railway

e: A debit balance under a suspense head represents an amount recoverable by, or awaiting adjustment in favour of, the Railway, so it is shown on the assets side of the Balance Sheet.

q: Deposits lying in the Public Account of India which remain unclaimed for more than three years are:

options.A: Refunded to the Reserve Bank of India
options.B: Transferred to the Contingency Fund of India
options.C: Held permanently as deposits of the Government
options.D: Credited to the revenues of the Government as lapsed deposits

e: Deposits lying in the Public Account which remain unclaimed for more than three years lapse and are credited to the revenues of the Government as lapsed deposits.

q: The collections under the small savings schemes of the Government of India are credited to:

options.A: The National Small Savings Fund, forming part of the Public Account of India
options.B: The Consolidated Fund of India as tax revenue
options.C: The Contingency Fund of India
options.D: The Post Office Savings Bank only, outside the Government accounts

e: Small savings collections are not Government revenue but public moneys held for the depositors, and are credited to the National Small Savings Fund forming part of the Public Account of India.

q: 'Ways and Means Advances' to the Government of India are:

options.A: Loans granted by international financial institutions for budgetary support
options.B: Advances made by the Reserve Bank of India to meet temporary mismatches between the receipts and the payments of the Government
options.C: Advances granted to Government servants for house building
options.D: Market borrowings raised through dated securities

e: Ways and Means Advances are advances made by the Reserve Bank of India to enable the Government to tide over temporary mismatches between its receipts and its payments.

q: Volume I of the Indian Railway Accounts Code deals principally with:

options.A: Traffic accounts and the accounting of earnings
options.B: The general principles of railway accounting, the books of account and the compilation of accounts, other than traffic accounts
options.C: Stores accounts and stock verification
options.D: Workshop manufacturing accounts

e: Volume I of the Indian Railway Accounts Code deals with the general principles of railway accounting, the books of account and the compilation of accounts, other than traffic accounts.

q: The Railway Accounts Department, which compiles the accounts of Indian Railways, is manned principally by officers of:

options.A: The Indian Audit and Accounts Service
options.B: The Indian Railway Accounts Service
options.C: The Indian Civil Accounts Service
options.D: The Indian Revenue Service

e: The Railway Accounts Department, which compiles the accounts of Indian Railways, is manned principally by officers of the Indian Railway Accounts Service.

q: Consequent upon the merger of the Railway Budget with the General Budget, the practice which has been discontinued is:

options.A: Voting of the Demands for Grants of the Ministry of Railways
options.B: Presentation of a separate Railway Budget to Parliament by the Railway Minister
options.C: Preparation of Appropriation Accounts of Railways
options.D: Audit of railway accounts by the Comptroller and Auditor General

e: Consequent upon the merger of the Railway Budget with the General Budget, the presentation of a separate Railway Budget to Parliament by the Railway Minister was discontinued.

q: The Railway Convention Committee of 1949 recommended that the dividend payable by Railways to General Finances should be at the rate of:

options.A: 3 per cent per annum on the capital-at-charge
options.B: 5 per cent per annum on the capital-at-charge
options.C: 6 per cent per annum on the capital-at-charge
options.D: 4 per cent per annum on the capital-at-charge

e: The Railway Convention Committee of 1949 recommended that the dividend payable by Railways to General Finances be at the rate of 4 per cent per annum on the capital-at-charge.

q: The dividend payable by Railways to General Finances under the pre-merger convention represented, in substance:

options.A: A return on the capital invested in Railways out of the general revenues of the Government of India
options.B: A tax on the earnings of Railways
options.C: A penalty for the losses of Railways
options.D: The share of the States in railway earnings

e: The dividend represented, in substance, a return on the capital invested in the Railways out of the general revenues of the Government of India.

q: In the commercial accounts of Railways under the pre-merger system, the dividend payable to General Finances was treated as:

options.A: An item of ordinary working expenses
options.B: A charge on the Depreciation Reserve Fund
options.C: An appropriation out of the net revenue of Railways, and not as an item of working expenses
options.D: A deduction from the capital-at-charge

e: The dividend was an appropriation out of the net revenue of the Railways, payable after working expenses and fund appropriations were met; it was not itself an item of working expenses, and the balance left was the surplus.

q: Appropriations from revenue to the Railway Pension Fund are assessed on the basis of:

options.A: The rate of dividend payable to General Finances
options.B: The savings available in the revenue budget of the year
options.C: The number of trains run during the year
options.D: Actuarial valuation of the pensionary liabilities of Railways

e: Appropriations from revenue to the Railway Pension Fund are assessed on the basis of an actuarial valuation of the pensionary liabilities of the Railways, so that the fund is built up on a scientific basis.

q:
Consider the following statements:
1. The cost of rolling stock procured in replacement of condemned or over-aged stock is charged to the Depreciation Reserve Fund.
2. The cost of additional rolling stock procured to meet the growth of traffic is charged to Capital or financed from the Capital Fund/Extra Budgetary Resources.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 1 only
options.B: 2 only
options.C: Both 1 and 2
options.D: Neither 1 nor 2

e: Both are correct: the cost of rolling stock replacing condemned or over-aged stock is charged to the Depreciation Reserve Fund, while additional stock for growth of traffic is charged to Capital or financed from the Capital Fund or Extra Budgetary Resources.

q: The Performance Efficiency Index is regarded as a better basis than the Operating Ratio for comparing the efficiency of different railways, because:

options.A: It is expressed in absolute figures
options.B: Being built up from physical input and output parameters, it is not distorted by changes in fares, freight rates and the prices of inputs
options.C: It takes the dividend payable into account
options.D: It is computed only from the published Finance Accounts

e: The Performance Efficiency Index is built up from physical input and output parameters, so unlike the Operating Ratio it is not distorted by changes in fares, freight rates and the prices of inputs.

q: An Operating Ratio of exactly 100 per cent for a railway signifies that:

options.A: The gross working expenses are exactly equal to the gross traffic earnings, leaving no net revenue
options.B: The railway has earned a net revenue equal to its gross earnings
options.C: The capital-at-charge has been fully repaid
options.D: The working expenses are double the gross earnings

e: An Operating Ratio of exactly 100 per cent means the gross working expenses are exactly equal to the gross traffic earnings, leaving no net revenue at all.

q: A zonal railway has gross traffic earnings of Rs 5,000 crore and gross working expenses of Rs 4,600 crore. Its Operating Ratio is:
e: Operating Ratio = gross working expenses / gross traffic earnings x 100 = 4,600 / 5,000 x 100 = 92 per cent.

q: A railway has gross traffic earnings of Rs 6,000 crore and working expenses, including appropriations to the Depreciation Reserve Fund and the Pension Fund, of Rs 5,400 crore. Its net revenue is:

options.A: Rs 600 crore
options.B: Rs 500 crore
options.C: Rs 1,200 crore
options.D: Nil

e: Net revenue = gross traffic earnings - working expenses = 6,000 - 5,400 = Rs 600 crore.

q: The net revenue of a railway is Rs 1,050 crore and its capital-at-charge is Rs 15,000 crore. The return on capital-at-charge is:
e: Return on capital-at-charge = net revenue / capital-at-charge x 100 = 1,050 / 15,000 x 100 = 7 per cent.

q: Under the pre-merger financial convention, a railway had gross traffic earnings of Rs 5,000 crore, working expenses (including appropriations to the Depreciation Reserve Fund and the Pension Fund) of Rs 4,600 crore and dividend payable to General Finances of Rs 150 crore. Its surplus was:

options.A: Rs 400 crore
options.B: Rs 150 crore
options.C: Rs 550 crore
options.D: Rs 250 crore

e: Net revenue = 5,000 - 4,600 = Rs 400 crore; surplus = net revenue - dividend payable = 400 - 150 = Rs 250 crore.

q: A motion expressing want of confidence in the Council of Ministers can be moved only in:

options.A: The Rajya Sabha
options.B: The Lok Sabha
options.C: Either House of Parliament
options.D: A joint sitting of the two Houses

e: The Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha alone, so a motion expressing want of confidence in it can be moved only in the Lok Sabha.

q: The Finance Bill, which gives effect to the taxation proposals of the Budget, must be passed by Parliament and receive the assent of the President within:

options.A: 30 days of its introduction
options.B: 60 days of its introduction
options.C: 75 days of its introduction
options.D: 90 days of its introduction

e: The taxes proposed in the Budget are collected provisionally from the Budget day, and that provisional authority lapses unless the Finance Bill is passed by Parliament and assented to within 75 days of its introduction.

q:
Consider the following statements:
1. A Financial Bill of the first category, which contains any of the matters specified in Article 110 together with other matters, can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha and only with the recommendation of the President.
2. A Financial Bill of the second category, which involves expenditure from the Consolidated Fund of India but contains no matter specified in Article 110, can be introduced in either House, but it cannot be passed by either House unless the President has recommended its consideration.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 1 only
options.B: 2 only
options.C: Both 1 and 2
options.D: Neither 1 nor 2

e: Both are correct: a first-category Financial Bill can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha, and only with the President's recommendation; a second-category Bill may start in either House but cannot be passed unless the President has recommended its consideration.

q: The Annual Financial Statement, after its presentation, is laid before:

options.A: Both Houses of Parliament
options.B: The Lok Sabha only
options.C: The Rajya Sabha only
options.D: The Public Accounts Committee

e: The Annual Financial Statement is caused to be laid before both Houses of Parliament, though the Demands for Grants arising out of it are voted only by the Lok Sabha.

q: Demands for Grants are presented to the Lok Sabha only in respect of:

options.A: Charged expenditure on the Consolidated Fund of India
options.B: Expenditure met from the Public Account of India
options.C: Expenditure met from the Contingency Fund of India
options.D: Voted expenditure; charged expenditure, though shown in the Annual Financial Statement, is not presented in the form of Demands for Grants

e: Demands for Grants are presented only for voted expenditure; charged expenditure, though shown in the Annual Financial Statement, is not presented in the form of Demands and is not voted.

q: The Annual Financial Statement (Union Budget) is prepared by:

options.A: The Budget Division of the Department of Economic Affairs, Ministry of Finance
options.B: The Comptroller and Auditor General of India
options.C: The Controller General of Accounts
options.D: The NITI Aayog

e: The Annual Financial Statement of the Union is prepared by the Budget Division of the Department of Economic Affairs in the Ministry of Finance, which coordinates the estimates received from all Ministries.

q: Which of the following is NOT a Budget document presented to Parliament along with the Annual Financial Statement?

options.A: The Appropriation Accounts
options.B: The Budget at a Glance
options.C: The Expenditure Budget
options.D: The Finance Bill

e: The Appropriation Accounts are the audited accounts of a completed year, prepared after the accounts are closed; Budget at a Glance, the Expenditure Budget and the Finance Bill are the documents presented with the Budget.

q: The 'Outcome Budget' presented by the Ministries seeks primarily to:

options.A: Show the Demands for Grants Ministry-wise
options.B: List the tax proposals of the Government
options.C: Link the financial outlays provided in the Budget with the measurable outcomes and deliverables expected from them
options.D: Present the accounts of the previous year

e: The Outcome Budget links the financial outlays provided for the schemes of a Ministry with the measurable outcomes and deliverables expected from them, so that results can be judged against the money provided.

q: Performance budgeting, as distinct from traditional line-item budgeting, lays emphasis on:

options.A: The objects of expenditure alone, such as salaries and stores
options.B: The items of receipts of the Government
options.C: Only the capital expenditure of the Government
options.D: The physical targets and achievements of programmes and activities in relation to the financial outlays on them

e: Performance budgeting lays emphasis on the physical targets and achievements of programmes and activities in relation to the financial outlays on them, unlike traditional budgeting which stresses only the objects of expenditure.

q: The six-tier structure of classification of Government accounts, in descending order, is:

options.A: Major Head, Minor Head, Sector, Sub-Major Head, Sub Head, Detailed Head
options.B: Sector, Sub-Major Head, Major Head, Sub Head, Minor Head, Detailed Head
options.C: Major Head, Sub-Major Head, Minor Head, Detailed Head, Sub Head, Sector
options.D: Sector, Major Head, Sub-Major Head, Minor Head, Sub Head, Detailed Head

e: The six-tier classification of Government accounts descends in the order: Sector, Major Head, Sub-Major Head, Minor Head, Sub Head and Detailed Head, from the broadest function to the most detailed unit.

q: The List of Major and Minor Heads of Account, which prescribes the classification of the transactions of the Government, is issued by:

options.A: The Comptroller and Auditor General of India directly
options.B: The Controller General of Accounts in the Ministry of Finance
options.C: The Railway Board, in the case of railway transactions
options.D: The Public Accounts Committee

e: The List of Major and Minor Heads of Account, which prescribes the classification of Government transactions, is issued by the Controller General of Accounts in the Ministry of Finance.

q: Treasury Bills, through which the Government of India raises short-term funds, are issued on behalf of the Government by:

options.A: The State Bank of India
options.B: The Controller General of Accounts
options.C: The Reserve Bank of India
options.D: The Indian Railway Finance Corporation

e: Treasury Bills, through which the Government of India raises short-term funds, are issued on its behalf by the Reserve Bank of India.

q:
Consider the following statements:
1. Treasury Bills issued by the Government of India form part of its external debt.
2. Market loans raised by the Government of India within the country form part of its internal debt.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 1 only
options.B: 2 only
options.C: Both 1 and 2
options.D: Neither 1 nor 2

e: Statement 1 is false: Treasury Bills are raised within the country and form part of internal debt, not external debt. Statement 2 is correct: market loans raised within the country form part of internal debt.

q: The Comptroller and Auditor General of India is often described as:

options.A: The financial adviser to Parliament
options.B: The chief accounting authority of the Union
options.C: The disbursing authority for the Consolidated Fund of India
options.D: The guardian or watchdog of the public purse

e: The Comptroller and Auditor General is described as the guardian or watchdog of the public purse because his audit ensures that public money is raised and spent only as authorised by the Legislature.

q: Besides the Reports on the Appropriation Accounts and the Finance Accounts of the Union, the Comptroller and Auditor General of India submits to the President a separate Report relating to:

options.A: The accounts of the State Governments
options.B: The Demands for Grants of the Ministries
options.C: The outcome budgets of the Ministries
options.D: The accounts of Government companies and public undertakings (commercial audit)

e: Besides the Reports on the Appropriation Accounts and the Finance Accounts of the Union, the Comptroller and Auditor General submits a separate Report relating to the accounts of Government companies and public undertakings, that is, commercial audit.

q: The Appropriation Accounts of the Union, including those relating to Railways, are:

options.A: Prepared by the accounting organisation of the Government/Railways and audited and certified by the Comptroller and Auditor General of India
options.B: Prepared by the Comptroller and Auditor General of India himself
options.C: Prepared by the Public Accounts Committee
options.D: Prepared by the Ministry of Finance and audited by the Reserve Bank of India

e: The Appropriation Accounts are prepared by the accounting organisation of the Government or the Railways concerned and are audited and certified by the Comptroller and Auditor General; he does not prepare them himself.

q: The control exercised by the Public Accounts Committee over public expenditure is essentially:

options.A: Prior control, exercised before the expenditure is incurred
options.B: Concurrent control, exercised while the expenditure is being incurred
options.C: Post-expenditure (post-mortem) control, exercised after the moneys have been spent, on the basis of the accounts and the Audit Reports
options.D: Control over the policy underlying the expenditure

e: The control of the Public Accounts Committee is post-expenditure, or post-mortem, control: it examines the accounts and the Audit Reports after the moneys have been spent, and not before or during expenditure.

q: In a performance audit conducted by the Comptroller and Auditor General of India, an 'exit conference' is held in order to:

options.A: Decide the programme of audit for the next year
options.B: Discuss the draft audit findings and observations with the audited entity before the Report is finalised
options.C: Present the Report to Parliament
options.D: Settle the fees payable for the audit

e: An exit conference is held at the close of a performance audit to discuss the draft audit findings and observations with the audited entity and obtain its response before the Report is finalised.

q: According to the auditing standards followed by the Comptroller and Auditor General of India, the audit evidence obtained should be:

options.A: Sufficient in quantity and appropriate in quality to support the audit conclusions
options.B: Based only on the oral statements of the audited staff
options.C: Collected only from documents of the last month of the year
options.D: Confined to transactions above a value fixed by Parliament

e: The audit evidence obtained should be sufficient in quantity and appropriate in quality, that is, relevant and reliable, so as to support the audit conclusions.

q: The Information Systems (IT) audit conducted by the organisation of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India is concerned mainly with examining:

options.A: The controls, security, reliability and integrity of computerised systems through which transactions are processed
options.B: The physical stock of stores held in depots
options.C: The punctuality of train services
options.D: The recruitment of staff to computer cadres

e: Information Systems audit is concerned mainly with examining the controls, security, reliability and integrity of the computerised systems through which transactions are processed.

q: An environment audit conducted by the Comptroller and Auditor General of India examines, among other things:

options.A: The landscape plans of Government office buildings
options.B: The colour schemes prescribed for Government offices
options.C: The compliance of Government programmes with environmental laws and the performance of the Government in protecting the environment
options.D: The weather forecasts issued by the Government

e: Environment audit examines, among other things, the compliance of Government programmes with environmental laws and the performance of the Government in protecting the environment.

q: In Indian Railways, IPAS, the application through which the compilation of accounts and the payroll of railway employees are processed, stands for:

options.A: Indian Passenger Amenities System
options.B: Integrated Payroll and Accounting System
options.C: Integrated Passenger Accounting System
options.D: Internal Payment and Adjustment System

e: IPAS stands for Integrated Payroll and Accounting System, the application through which the payroll of railway employees and the compilation of accounts are processed.

q:
Consider the following statements:
1. The appropriation to the Depreciation Reserve Fund is charged to the working expenses of the Railways before arriving at the net revenue.
2. The appropriation to the Development Fund is likewise charged to the working expenses of the Railways.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 1 only
options.B: 2 only
options.C: Both 1 and 2
options.D: Neither 1 nor 2

e: Statement 1 is correct: the appropriation to the Depreciation Reserve Fund is charged to the working expenses before arriving at net revenue. Statement 2 is false: the Development Fund is fed out of the surplus and is not charged to working expenses.

q: A zonal railway has gross traffic earnings of Rs 2,400 crore, ordinary working expenses of Rs 1,900 crore, appropriation to the Depreciation Reserve Fund of Rs 100 crore and appropriation to the Pension Fund of Rs 100 crore. Dividend payable to General Finances is Rs 120 crore. Its net revenue and surplus are respectively:

options.A: Rs 500 crore and Rs 380 crore
options.B: Rs 300 crore and Rs 120 crore
options.C: Rs 250 crore and Rs 130 crore
options.D: Rs 300 crore and Rs 180 crore

e: Net revenue = 2,400 - (1,900 + 100 + 100) = Rs 300 crore; surplus = net revenue - dividend = 300 - 120 = Rs 180 crore.

q: A zonal railway has gross traffic earnings of Rs 3,000 crore and working expenses, including appropriations to the Depreciation Reserve Fund and the Pension Fund, of Rs 2,850 crore. The dividend payable by it to General Finances is Rs 200 crore. The position of the railway is that:

options.A: It has earned a surplus of Rs 50 crore after payment of dividend
options.B: Its net revenue is Rs 150 crore, leaving a shortfall of Rs 50 crore against the dividend liability
options.C: Its net revenue is Rs 200 crore and there is neither surplus nor shortfall
options.D: Its Operating Ratio is 105 per cent

e: Net revenue = 3,000 - 2,850 = Rs 150 crore, which falls short of the dividend liability of Rs 200 crore by Rs 50 crore, so the railway has a shortfall and no surplus.

q: A zonal railway has gross traffic earnings of Rs 8,000 crore, ordinary working expenses of Rs 6,200 crore, appropriation to the Depreciation Reserve Fund of Rs 400 crore and appropriation to the Pension Fund of Rs 400 crore. Its Operating Ratio is:

options.A: 77.5 per cent
options.B: 85 per cent
options.C: 87.5 per cent
options.D: 90 per cent

e: Gross working expenses = 6,200 + 400 + 400 = Rs 7,000 crore; Operating Ratio = 7,000 / 8,000 x 100 = 87.5 per cent.

q:
Consider the following statements:
1. The fiscal deficit of the Government for a year represents, in substance, the total borrowing requirement of the Government for that year.
2. The fiscal deficit is the excess of the revenue expenditure of the Government over its revenue receipts.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 1 only
options.B: 2 only
options.C: Both 1 and 2
options.D: Neither 1 nor 2

e: Statement 1 is correct: the fiscal deficit represents, in substance, the total borrowing requirement of the Government for the year. Statement 2 is false: the excess of revenue expenditure over revenue receipts is the revenue deficit.

q: The 'primary deficit' of the Government for a year is arrived at by deducting, from the fiscal deficit of that year:

options.A: The revenue receipts
options.B: The capital expenditure
options.C: The disinvestment proceeds
options.D: The interest payments

e: The primary deficit is arrived at by deducting the interest payments from the fiscal deficit, so it shows the year's borrowing requirement apart from interest on past borrowings.

q: Under the Constitution, the administrative expenses of the Supreme Court, including the salaries, allowances and pensions payable to its officers and servants, are:

options.A: Voted by the Lok Sabha every year
options.B: Charged on the Consolidated Fund of India
options.C: Met from the Public Account of India
options.D: Met from the Contingency Fund of India

e: The administrative expenses of the Supreme Court, including the salaries, allowances and pensions of its officers and servants, are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India and are not voted by Parliament.

q: The salaries and allowances of the Speaker and the Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha and of the Chairman and the Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha are:

options.A: Charged on the Consolidated Fund of India
options.B: Voted as part of the Demands for Grants of the Ministry of Parliamentary Affairs
options.C: Paid out of the Public Account of India
options.D: Fixed by the Finance Commission

e: The salaries and allowances of the Speaker and the Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha and of the Chairman and the Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India.

q: A joint sitting of the two Houses of Parliament, provided for resolving a deadlock over a Bill, cannot be held in the case of:

options.A: An ordinary Bill
options.B: A Financial Bill of the second category
options.C: A Money Bill
options.D: A Bill passed again by the Lok Sabha after rejection by the Rajya Sabha

e: A joint sitting is meant to resolve a deadlock between the two Houses, but it cannot be held for a Money Bill, over which the Lok Sabha's decision prevails and the Rajya Sabha can only make recommendations.

q: After the Demands for Grants have been voted by the Lok Sabha, the Appropriation Bill introduced to authorise appropriation from the Consolidated Fund of India is treated as:

options.A: An ordinary Bill
options.B: A Money Bill
options.C: A Constitution Amendment Bill
options.D: A private member's Bill

e: The Appropriation Bill authorises appropriation out of the Consolidated Fund of India, which is a Money Bill matter, and it is accordingly treated as a Money Bill.

q: In respect of the moneys held in the Public Account of India, the position is that:

options.A: Every payment out of it requires a Demand for Grant to be voted by the Lok Sabha
options.B: Every payment out of it requires an Appropriation Act
options.C: It can be operated only with the prior permission of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India
options.D: Payments out of it, the Government holding the moneys as trustee or banker, do not require appropriation by Parliament

e: The moneys in the Public Account are held by the Government as trustee or banker, so payments out of it do not require appropriation by Parliament.

q: The Provident Fund balances of Government servants, to which the Government stands in the position of a trustee, are accounted for in:

options.A: The Public Account of India
options.B: The Consolidated Fund of India as a capital receipt
options.C: The Contingency Fund of India
options.D: The Finance Accounts as a revenue receipt

e: Provident Fund balances of Government servants are moneys to which the Government stands in the position of a trustee, and are therefore accounted for in the Public Account of India.

q: 'Remittance heads' in the Government system of accounts are operated mainly to account for:

options.A: The salaries remitted to the bank accounts of employees
options.B: The profits remitted by public undertakings to the Government
options.C: Transactions which are in transit between two accounting circles, such as cash or cheques sent by one office and awaiting acknowledgment or encashment at the other
options.D: The taxes remitted by the Union to the States

e: Remittance heads are operated mainly for transactions which are in transit between two accounting circles, such as cash or cheques sent by one office and awaiting acknowledgment or encashment at the other.

q: Personal Deposit accounts, opened in Government accounts for officers administering funds of local bodies and similar moneys, are maintained as part of:

options.A: The Consolidated Fund of India
options.B: The Contingency Fund of India
options.C: The Public Account of India
options.D: The Depreciation Reserve Fund

e: Personal Deposit accounts, opened for officers administering funds of local bodies and similar moneys, are maintained as part of the Public Account of India.

q: A 'permanent advance' (imprest) sanctioned in favour of a Government officer is intended to enable him to:

options.A: Draw his salary in advance every month
options.B: Make advances to contractors before execution of works
options.C: Lend money to subordinate staff in emergencies
options.D: Meet petty contingent expenditure of his office, the amount being recouped on submission of the bills

e: A permanent advance, or imprest, enables an officer to meet petty contingent expenditure of his office as it arises, the amount being recouped on submission of the bills.

q: Where an error in the classification of a transaction is noticed after the accounts of the month have been closed, it is rectified in Government and Railway accounts by:

options.A: A transfer entry in the accounts of a subsequent month, the closed accounts not being reopened
options.B: Reopening and rewriting the closed accounts of that month
options.C: Treating the amount as a fresh receipt of the current year
options.D: Writing off the amount with the sanction of the Finance Ministry

e: Closed accounts are not reopened; an error in classification noticed after the month's accounts have closed is rectified by a transfer entry in the accounts of a subsequent month.

q: In respect of the accounts of Railways (as also of Defence), the Comptroller and Auditor General of India stands relieved of the responsibility of compilation, and accordingly the accounts of Railways are:

options.A: Compiled by the Controller General of Accounts
options.B: Compiled by the Reserve Bank of India
options.C: Compiled by the Railway Accounts Department, while audit remains with the Comptroller and Auditor General of India
options.D: Compiled by the Public Accounts Committee

e: In respect of Railways, as also of Defence, the Comptroller and Auditor General stands relieved of the responsibility of compilation; railway accounts are compiled by the Railway Accounts Department, while audit remains with him.

q: The office of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India is an authority consisting of:

options.A: A Chairman and four members appointed by the President
options.B: Three members elected by Parliament
options.C: A Board constituted by the Finance Ministry
options.D: A single person, the Comptroller and Auditor General, assisted by the Indian Audit and Accounts Department

e: The office of the Comptroller and Auditor General is a single-person authority, the Comptroller and Auditor General himself, assisted by the Indian Audit and Accounts Department.

q: The accounts and reports of railway public sector undertakings, such as the Rail Vikas Nigam Limited and IRCON International Limited, are examined by:

options.A: The Railway Convention Committee
options.B: The Estimates Committee
options.C: The Departmentally Related Standing Committee on Railways only
options.D: The Committee on Public Undertakings

e: The accounts and reports of railway public sector undertakings, such as Rail Vikas Nigam Limited and IRCON International Limited, are examined by the Committee on Public Undertakings.

q: The 'Pink Book' of Indian Railways, presented as a Budget document, contains principally:

options.A: The Works, Machinery and Plant and Rolling Stock Programmes of the Railways, including the list of sanctioned works
options.B: The time tables of passenger trains
options.C: The rules for the reservation of accommodation
options.D: The list of railway stations and their earnings

e: The Pink Book contains principally the Works, Machinery and Plant and Rolling Stock Programmes of the Railways, including the list of sanctioned works, for the Budget year.

q: In a year in which a general election to the Lok Sabha is due, the Interim Budget presented to Parliament generally seeks:

options.A: Approval of the full year's Demands for Grants
options.B: A Vote on Account for the expenditure of the initial months of the financial year, pending presentation of the regular Budget by the new Government
options.C: An exceptional grant for the whole year
options.D: A Vote of Credit for the whole year

e: In a general election year, the Interim Budget generally seeks only a Vote on Account for the expenditure of the initial months of the financial year, pending presentation of the regular Budget by the new Government.

q: The Economic Survey, which reviews the developments in the economy over the previous year, is prepared and tabled in Parliament before the presentation of the Union Budget by:

options.A: The Reserve Bank of India
options.B: The Department of Economic Affairs, Ministry of Finance
options.C: The Central Statistical Organisation alone
options.D: The Finance Commission

e: The Economic Survey, which reviews the developments in the economy over the previous year, is prepared by the Department of Economic Affairs and tabled in Parliament before the presentation of the Union Budget.

q: 'Proforma accounts' are prepared in Government and Railway accounting in respect of:

options.A: Every ordinary office of the Government
options.B: Departmental commercial undertakings, such as railway printing presses, so that their commercial results can be ascertained separately
options.C: The personal accounts of Government servants
options.D: The accounts of private contractors executing Government works

e: Proforma accounts are prepared in respect of departmental commercial undertakings, such as railway printing presses, so that their commercial results can be ascertained separately from the general accounts.

q: The Constitution of India does not use the word 'Budget' anywhere; the annual budget of the Union is referred to in the Constitution as the:

options.A: Finance Bill
options.B: Demands for Grants
options.C: Annual Financial Statement
options.D: Appropriation Statement

e: The Constitution does not use the word Budget anywhere; the annual budget of the Union is referred to in it as the Annual Financial Statement.

q: The Finance Commission constituted under Article 280 of the Constitution consists of:

options.A: A Chairman and five other members
options.B: A Chairman and four other members
options.C: A Chairman and six other members
options.D: Only a Chairman, without any members

e: The Finance Commission consists of a Chairman and four other members, five persons in all, appointed by the President.

q: The First Finance Commission of India, chaired by Shri K. C. Neogy, was constituted in the year:
e: The First Finance Commission, chaired by Shri K. C. Neogy, was constituted in 1951, shortly after the Constitution came into force, to make the first recommendations on sharing of taxes with the States.

q: Grants made by the Union under Article 282 of the Constitution differ from grants-in-aid under Article 275 in that grants under Article 282:

options.A: Are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India
options.B: Are made only on the recommendation of the Finance Commission
options.C: Require the prior approval of the Public Accounts Committee
options.D: May be made for any public purpose, even for a purpose outside the legislative competence of the Union

e: Grants under Article 282 may be made for any public purpose, even for a purpose outside the legislative competence of the Union, unlike grants-in-aid under Article 275 which are need-based grants to States.

q: When a Money Bill is presented to the President for his assent, the President:

options.A: May return the Bill to Parliament for reconsideration
options.B: May give his assent or withhold it, but cannot return the Bill for reconsideration
options.C: Must return the Bill if the Rajya Sabha has made recommendations on it
options.D: Refers the Bill to the Supreme Court for its opinion

e: When a Money Bill is presented for assent, the President may give his assent or withhold it, but he cannot return the Bill to Parliament for reconsideration, a course open to him only for other Bills.

q: The Goods and Services Tax Council, which makes recommendations to the Union and the States on the taxes, rates and principles of GST, is constituted under:

options.A: Article 269
options.B: Article 270
options.C: Article 279A
options.D: Article 280

e: The Goods and Services Tax Council, which makes recommendations to the Union and the States on the taxes, rates and principles of GST, is constituted under Article 279A of the Constitution.

q: Besides the Appropriation Accounts of the Union Government and the Reports of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India thereon, the Public Accounts Committee also examines:

options.A: The Finance Accounts of the Union Government
options.B: The estimates of the Ministries before they are voted
options.C: The annual reports of public undertakings
options.D: The Demands for Grants of the Ministry of Railways

e: Besides the Appropriation Accounts of the Union Government and the Audit Reports thereon, the Public Accounts Committee also examines the Finance Accounts of the Union Government.

q: A Minister is not eligible to be a member of:

options.A: The Public Accounts Committee
options.B: The Estimates Committee
options.C: The Committee on Public Undertakings
options.D: Any of the three Financial Committees of Parliament

e: A Minister is not eligible to be a member of any of the three Financial Committees of Parliament, so that the Legislature's financial control over the executive remains independent of the executive itself.

q: The members of the Committee on Public Undertakings hold office for a term of:

options.A: One year
options.B: Three years
options.C: Five years
options.D: Two years

e: The Committee on Public Undertakings is constituted afresh every year and its members accordingly hold office for a term of one year.

q: The Chairperson of the Committee on Public Undertakings is:

options.A: Appointed by the Speaker from amongst the members of the Committee who are members of the Lok Sabha
options.B: Elected by the members of the Committee from amongst themselves
options.C: Nominated by the President of India
options.D: The Minister of Heavy Industries, ex-officio

e: The Chairperson of the Committee on Public Undertakings is appointed by the Speaker from amongst the members of the Committee who are members of the Lok Sabha.
